final_proof:
Assume first that a < b. Since f is continuous on [a,b], it is Riemann integrable on every closed subinterval of [a,b], so F(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt is well defined for every x ∈ [a,b].

Fix x ∈ (a,b). If h ≠ 0 is sufficiently small that x+h ∈ [a,b], additivity of the integral gives

F(x+h) − F(x) = ∫_a^(x+h) f(t) dt − ∫_a^x f(t) dt = ∫_x^(x+h) f(t) dt.

Consequently, using ∫_x^(x+h) f(x) dt = h f(x) (with the usual orientation when h < 0),

(F(x+h) − F(x))/h − f(x) = (1/h) ∫_x^(x+h) (f(t) − f(x)) dt.

Let ε > 0. By continuity of f at x, there is δ₀ > 0 such that

|f(t) − f(x)| < ε whenever t ∈ [a,b] and |t−x| < δ₀.

Choose δ > 0 smaller than δ₀, x−a, and b−x. For 0 < |h| < δ, every t between x and x+h satisfies |t−x| ≤ |h| < δ₀. If I_h denotes the unoriented interval having endpoints x and x+h, then the standard integral estimate yields

|(F(x+h) − F(x))/h − f(x)| ≤ (1/|h|) ∫_(I_h) |f(t) − f(x)| dt ≤ (1/|h|)(ε|h|) = ε.

Thus

F′(x) = lim_(h→0) (F(x+h) − F(x))/h = f(x).

Since x was arbitrary, F′ = f throughout (a,b). This is precisely the usual meaning of saying that F is a primitive of f on the closed interval [a,b].

If differentiability on a closed interval is defined to include one-sided derivatives at its endpoints, the same calculation also supplies them. For h > 0, continuity of f at a relative to [a,b] gives

lim_(h↓0) (F(a+h) − F(a))/h = f(a),

and for h < 0, continuity at b gives

lim_(h↑0) (F(b+h) − F(b))/h = f(b).

Hence the right derivative at a and the left derivative at b equal f(a) and f(b), respectively. Therefore, under either standard endpoint convention, F is a primitive of f on [a,b]. If the degenerate interval a = b is allowed, its interior is empty, so the assertion is vacuous under the usual definition (and F(a) = 0).
